transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Lee. Well, I'm here because I just keep snapping at people. I work as an inspector, and lately... I don't know, I just lose my temper so fast. Like at our last safety meeting, I started yelling before I could even stop myself. It's gotten to the point where the younger inspectors act scared to even ask me anything about the line. I just need to figure out what's going on with me.
How long has this pattern of quick temper and snapping at people been going on—did it start suddenly a few weeks ago, or has it been more of a lifelong pattern for you?

No, it's definitely not a lifelong thing, and it wasn't just a few weeks ago either. It started... well, it's been going on since that machinery accident we had right after the overnight schedule change. That was about two years and four months ago now.
During that machinery accident, did you hit your head, lose consciousness, or sustain any injury to your head?
No, I didn't. I wasn't the one who got hurt. I was just there when it happened. I didn't hit my head or get injured at all.
Since the accident, have you found yourself having unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about what happened that day?

Yes, I do. It doesn't even take much to set it off. Just hearing a loud clank from a cart rolling by, or... or catching the smell of hot oil on the floor. It can put me right back in that bay. I just end up seeing my coworker right there by the machine, like... like it's happening in front of me all over again.
Since the accident, have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, or situations at work—like specific machinery or areas of the plant—that remind you of that day?

Yes, I do. I actually go out of my way not to pass the inspection bay at work anymore. And I really won't talk about the accident with anyone if I can help it. 

It's even spilled over into things I used to like doing on my own time. I used to really enjoy going to these local industrial-history talks, but I just quit going. Seeing the pictures of the old machinery... it just sets me off now, so I stay away from all of it.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a persistent, distressing symptom cluster that began after witnessing a traumatic machinery accident at work (a clear qualifying traumatic stressor) and has persisted for over two years, well beyond the one-month threshold required to differentiate PTSD from Acute Stress Disorder. Core symptoms include intrusive re-experiencing (unwanted memories, flashbacks triggered by sensory cues such as sounds and smells), avoidance (of the inspection bay, discussing the accident, and previously enjoyed activities), and hyperarousal/irritability (sudden anger outbursts, snapping at coworkers, causing them to feel afraid). This constellation aligns with classic PTSD criteria rather than a personality disorder or other anxiety condition, and there is no evidence of head injury or loss of consciousness to suggest a neurological etiology.
